title: Lawyer laments inquest delays: Hold hearings while 'memories are fresh'
article: Coroner's inquests into police shootings are needlessly delayed, says a lawyer involved in the case of a Vanderhoof man killed in 2004.

Cameron Ward is representing Rebecca Gingera, the girlfriend of Kevin St. Arnaud, 29, who was shot three times by a rookie Vanderhoof RCMP officer on Dec. 19, 2004. A mandatory inquest into the death has yet to be scheduled.
The family of Houston man Ian Bush, 22, who was shot last Oct. 29 by an officer just five months out of basic training, is also awaiting an inquest date.
"It is most unfortunate to the family members. In my view, it's wrong," Ward said.
He said inquests into police shootings used to be held within six months. Ward said he has seen a dramatic shift under the stewardship of current chief coroner Terry Smith.
"Many, many months, sometimes years, go by \[before inquests in such cases are called\]," said Ward. "An inquest should be quick. Memories are fresh."
Coroner's inquests are not fault-finding exercises, he said. Rather, they seek to determine only the facts of an incident.
The Coroner's Act provides legal protection for witnesses, Ward stressed, and there is nothing in official policy preventing them from being held sooner.
He believes an inquest is an excellent and complementary tool for whatever other agencies may be investigating a police shooting.
But Smith, a former RCMP chief, disputes Ward's claims.
Smith says inquests are more thorough when all incidental investigations are complete, because there is more information on the table.
Secondly, an inquest prior to criminal charges may impede the ability of Crown to proceed with a prosecution, he said.
Thirdly, a coroner's ability to compel evidence under oath from someone who may later be criminally charged may be difficult.
"There is nothing different between a \[coroner's inquest examining a police shooting\] and any other investigation we do," Smith said.
Crown counsel announced last week that an RCMP investigation of the shooting of St. Arnaud wouldn't result in charges against
Const. Ryan Sheremetta, who shot the intoxicated man.
In the meantime, the B.C. Civil Liberties Association is lobbying RCMP Commissioner Giuliano Zaccardelli and Public Safety
Minister Stockwell Day to make civilian reviews of in-custody deaths automatic.
The association contends that the Commission for Public Complaints against the RCMP is not living up to its mandate by its refusal to order investigations into the St. Arnaud and Bush incidents.
The association is calling on CPC commissioner Paul Kennedy to investigate both cases as well as the deaths in custody of two other B.C. men.
Ryan Glen Snopek died in a Cranbrook RCMP cell New Year's Day. Gurmeet Sandhu died in Surrey last June after he was Tasered by RCMP.
